article.title: At Hot Chips 2026, OpenAI Details Jalapeno Inference Chip, Claiming Up to 1.9x Better Throughput per Watt Than Nvidia's GB200
article.summary: OpenAI presented Jalapeno's first independently reported benchmarks at Hot Chips 2026, claiming higher tokens-per-watt than Nvidia's GB200 and GB300 on three open models.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

OpenAI used the second day of the Hot Chips 2026 conference to disclose the first independently reported technical details and benchmark data for Jalapeno, its custom inference chip built with Broadcom, according to [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/). Presenters Richard Ho, Ravi Narayanaswami, and Chris Leary walked through the chip's roughly nine-month path from initial RTL to tapeout, its performance positioning against Nvidia's GB200 and GB300 accelerators, and an architecture built around HBM4 memory and a spatial programming model, [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/) reported. [Tom's Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/hot-chips-2026-openais-jalapeno-ai-asic-unpacked-accelerator-developed-using-ai-achieves-efficiency-and-throughput-gains-against-power-hungry-blackwell) also covered the presentation, similarly describing the disclosed figures as efficiency and throughput gains over Nvidia's Blackwell-generation hardware. The disclosure fills a gap flagged when OpenAI and Broadcom first [unveiled Jalapeno in June](/article/2026-06/26-openai-and-broadcom-unveil-jalapeo-a-custom-llm-inference-chip-designed-in-nine-months-and-targeting-deployment-by-the-end-of-2026), when no technical report had been published and performance-per-watt claims were self-reported without supporting data.

## What We Know

The development timeline shown at Hot Chips traces an architecture concept in late 2024, an RTL freeze in 2025, a tapeout in late 2025, and Codex running on the silicon in early 2026, with ChatGPT deployment following not long after, according to [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/).

For performance, OpenAI presented results from InferenceX, which [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/) describes as "a public, power-normalized benchmark across a basket of open-source models that spans the full prefill-to-decode spectrum." Runs were normalized to package power, with Jalapeno rated at 700 watts against Nvidia's GB200 at 1.2 kilowatts and the GB300 and AMD's MI355X at 1.4 kilowatts, [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/) reported. OpenAI ran three open models through the benchmark: GPT-OSS 120B "to stress latency limits," DeepSeek R1 as "a good draft-model case," and the 1-trillion-parameter Kimi K2.5 to show "scaling across many devices," per [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/), which noted none of the three models were co-designed for Jalapeno.

On GPT-OSS 120B against the GB200, [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/) reported Jalapeno showed "about 1.9x higher peak mixed tokens per second per kilowatt and roughly 1.7x lower end-to-end latency," with "around 53.7x more throughput" at the previous best time-between-tokens measurement. On the larger DeepSeek R1 670B model in MXFP4 precision against the GB300, the gains widened: "about 1.7x higher peak mixed tokens per kilowatt per second and 3.6x lower end-to-end latency," and "roughly 104.3x more throughput" at the previous best time-between-tokens figure, according to [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/). On the trillion-parameter Kimi K2.5, [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/) reported Jalapeno reached "about 1.5x higher peak mixed tokens per second per kilowatt and 3.4x lower end-to-end latency, with roughly 56.1x higher throughput" than the prior best.

One methodology detail matters for reading those numbers: Jalapeno used single-token prediction in the tests, while the Nvidia baselines used multi-token prediction, according to [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/). OpenAI also ran a more direct comparison — Jalapeno in single-token mode against the GB300 in multi-token mode on DeepSeek R1 — and still reported "about 1.5x higher peak mixed-token rate per kilowatt and 2.2x lower end-to-end latency," a margin [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/) said "narrows relative to the plain GB300 comparison but remains clearly positive." OpenAI also claimed sub-millisecond token-to-token latency on frontier models at economical throughputs, and said multi-token prediction could add another "3x to 5x latency improvement at iso-efficiency," per [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/).

On the silicon itself, [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/) reported a single Jalapeno chip delivers 13.4 PFLOP/s of MXFP4 matrix compute, 15.4 TB/s of HBM4 bandwidth across 216 GiB of memory, in a 700-watt package. Scaled to a 2,048-chip system, that becomes 27 EFLOP/s and 432 TiB of memory, with 600 GB/s of network bandwidth inside a 128-chip local domain and 200 GB/s across the full 2,048-chip global domain, built on a "half-flattened two-level Clos topology" using Broadcom Tomahawk6 switches, [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/) reported.

OpenAI also detailed using its own internal AI model, paired with the XLS hardware description language, to help design the chip, with major changes landing "up to the day of the RTL freeze," according to [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/). Measured gains over a human design baseline included a 56 percent improvement on a BF16 multiply unit and a 10 percent smaller matrix unit area, per [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/). The chip runs on a spatial architecture in which OpenAI's Gluon framework "programs each physical core as a thread block," and an internal AI system generated attention and mixture-of-experts kernels that run "1.5x to 1.8x faster than existing expert-written implementations, validated end-to-end on-chip," [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/) reported.

OpenAI framed Jalapeno as "Gen 1 of a multi-generation roadmap," with a second generation targeting better performance per watt and a third aimed at economical, low-latency serving, according to [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/), which also noted OpenAI credited Broadcom and Celestica during the presentation.

## What We Don't Know

The benchmark results presented at Hot Chips are OpenAI's own InferenceX measurements, shown on OpenAI's own stage, and have not yet been independently reproduced by a third party. The single-token-versus-multi-token difference between Jalapeno and the Nvidia baselines complicates a direct read of the headline multipliers, even though OpenAI's own matched single-token comparison against the GB300 still showed a lead. [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/openai-jalapeno-asic-at-hot-chips-2026/) also reported a gap between theoretical and realized performance: Jalapeno's raw HBM4 bandwidth implies a ceiling of 1,000 to 2,000 tokens per second per user without speculative decoding, and 5,000 to 10,000 with it, but "OpenAI acknowledges the real system lands well below either rate," indicating bandwidth is not the only limiting factor. OpenAI has not published a full technical report on Jalapeno.

## Analysis

The Hot Chips presentation is the first time OpenAI has backed its inference-chip claims with specific, benchmarked figures rather than the general performance-per-watt language used at the June unveiling. That still leaves the numbers as vendor-reported results from a benchmark OpenAI itself designed and normalized, run against three models that were not built for Jalapeno's architecture. The methodology gap between single-token and multi-token prediction, which OpenAI addressed directly with its own matched comparison, is the kind of detail that will matter most once independent labs get access to the hardware and can test it against production inference stacks rather than a conference-stage demo.
